tagline: River highways and mountain bends share the name of a bestselling novel
intro: The Trail of the Lonesome Pine name appears on US 19 east of Lebanon and on Route 160 above Appalachia. The driving changes with the road: US 19 and US 460 parallel the Clinch River and its railway through Pounding Mill, then become a freeway through Tazewell. Route 160 climbs from Looney Creek toward Black Mountain through hairpin turns. South of Jonesville, Route 70 crosses Wallen Ridge and Powell Mountain, using Hunter Gap for the mountain crossing.

John Fox Jr.’s novel appeared in 1908 and became a bestseller. The same name belonged to an auto trail from Detroit to Florida, whose Jonesville–Blackwater section became part of Virginia’s highway system. In 1924, western Virginia residents asked the State Highway Commission to take over that road. The northern two miles entered the system that year; further additions followed in 1927 and 1928.

From Bluefield, US 19 and US 460 lead through Tazewell and Pounding Mill to Claypool Hill; US 19 continues toward Rosedale and Lebanon. Farther west, US 23 and Alternate 58 serve Norton and meet at Big Stone Gap. Big Stone Gap holds Fox’s former home. For the northbound branch, US 23 crosses Pine Mountain at Pound Gap into Kentucky.

moments.title: Norton
moments.text: Prince’s Flats acquired a railroad president’s name in a bid to secure a depot. The president was Eckstein Norton of the Louisville and Nashville Railroad. The city lies along the Powell and Guest rivers, with US 23 and Alternate 58 among its main highways. Although surrounded by Wise County, Norton is an independent city outside the county’s government. The 2020 census counted 3,687 residents, making it Virginia’s least populous city at that census.

moments.title: John Fox Jr. House
moments.text: The house on Shawnee Avenue grew from a four-room cottage built in 1890 to a two-story home with 20 rooms. Fox lived here from 1890 until 1919 and wrote his best-known works here. He had come to the region with his brothers as a speculator and mineral developer in 1888, before turning from real estate to writing. The home became a museum in 1970, operated by the Lonesome Pine Arts and Crafts Association. It remains furnished as it was during the Fox family’s residence. The frame house rests on a stone foundation, beneath the rooms added to the original cottage.

moments.title: Pound Gap
moments.text: US 23 crosses Pine Mountain through a wind gap, a pass through which streams no longer flow. The crossing lies between Pound, Virginia, and Jenkins, Kentucky. In 1834, Kentucky’s General Assembly authorized improvements to the road from Mount Sterling to the gap. Livestock drivers used that route to move horses, hogs and cattle toward Virginia and other southern markets. Construction of a new US 23 section in 1998 exposed the Pine Mountain Pound Gap Thrust Fault. The Kentucky Society of Professional Geologists designated the gap Kentucky’s first Distinguished Geologic Site on September 26, 1998.
